corrections.why: The ratio cells hold 1/N and were multiplied into wheel speed, so a 7:1 reduction made the motor turn 7x slower than the wheel instead of 7x faster (49x low in power at gear 7). Divided by the cell instead.

Current was V_pack * PF * RPM / 1000: volts times rpm, with no mass, drag, rolling resistance or acceleration, so it could not tell a launch from a cruise. It now reads the road-load pack current, which does not depend on the gear, so all fifteen columns agree.
Power multiplied by motor efficiency (losses must raise the draw, so they divide) and applied sqrt(3) and power factor to the DC bus. It now reads the road-load pack power, MAX(F v, 0) / eta.
The range ran one row past its block into the next one.
The range ran one row past its block into the next one.
The block is divided by 1000, so it is kW; the adjacent Max row already said so.
Pack resistance is S x R_cell / P. The old cell left out the parallel strings (3x high for 3P), and it feeds every joule-heat and EMF figure.
Max joule heat carried an extra factor of the fuse rating that the matching Min cell does not (I² x A x ohm); now the same formula as B4.
I² R is in watts.
Summing instantaneous watts gives watts, scaled by the row count. Energy is the sum of P x dt; now in kWh.
TAN takes radians: TAN(20) is the tangent of 20 rad, 6.15x tan(20°). And the moment arm of a gear is its pitch RADIUS, so torque divides by half the pitch diameter.
Column G ends one row earlier.

V_pack x power x R_pack is volts x kW x ohms, not a voltage. Of the two voltages it could mean, only the pack's terminal voltage under load, V - I R, can be computed from what the workbook holds (a motor back-EMF needs a V/rpm constant the file does not have), and it uses the same pack voltage and resistance cells. Now V - I R with the road-load current, one row per profile sample.
